text: dsh-multitask 是面向 DSH Web 客户端的多代理工作模式：主对话负责理解需求、拆分任务和汇总结果，文件读取、命令执行与搜索等工作交给子代理。它注册标准、继承上下文、PTC 和只读四类 worker，也可把任务派给其他已安装的 agent preset；协调者保留只读检查和委派工具，并提供子代理审批转发、工作区元数据查看、模型选择及并行度设置。适合希望把执行过程与主对话分开的开发和调研任务。需要 DSH 及其子代理服务，不需要额外 API 密钥。

dsh-multitask is a multi-agent mode for DSH web. The main chat plans and summarizes while subagents execute tasks. It provides four worker types, cross-mode dispatch, approval relays, and worker model settings. For development and research workflows. Requires DSH and its subagent service.

dsh-multitask 的功能「协调者工具范围」：主会话使用 Multitask preset 后保留只读检查、委派和结果管理等工具；执行型任务可由 worker 处理。该模式通过 preset 对会话工具目录进行配置。
dsh-multitask 的功能「四类子代理」：提供标准、继承已完成上下文、PTC 和只读四种子代理路径，按任务形态分配工作；两种扩展后端由插件注册。
dsh-multitask 的功能「跨模式委派」：协调者可查看已注册的 agent preset 列表，并按 preset id 启动另一个模式的 worker，取得其子会话 id 与结果。
dsh-multitask 的功能「子代理审批转发」：当 worker 遇到需要确认的操作时，审批闸门可把请求转发到父会话等待处理，并提供失败通知路径。
dsh-multitask 的功能「只读文件元数据」：file_info 工具让协调者查询文件的元数据，支持对 worker 的结论作独立核对。
dsh-multitask 的功能「Worker 模型与运行限制设置」：浏览器设置页可统一或按 worker 类型选择模型，并配置最大递归深度和并行数量上限。

dsh-multitask README · dsh-multitask：A work mode for **DeepSeek Harness（DSH）** in which **the main conversation does exactly three things**: understand what you asked for, turn it into task briefs, and report back what the Subagents concluded. Every piece of process data — file contents, command output, build logs, search results, dead ends — is digested inside a **Subagent's context** and never enters the main one. The main conversation therefore holds only high-value information.

dsh-multitask README · dsh-multitask：This is a **mechanism**, not a prompt asking the model to behave. Once the mode is selected, the main conversation (the coordinator) genuinely has a narrower tool surface: the tools that would drag in process data — writing files, running commands, searching the web — are **not in its visible set**. It cannot call them, so it cannot pollute its own context. A Subagent (worker) is the opposite: it gets the full tool surface, does the work, and returns only its conclusion.

dsh-multitask README · dsh-multitask：| Capability | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| Narrowed coordinator tool surface | the main conversation cannot write, run commands or search — those tools are genuinely absent, not merely discouraged |
| Process data never reaches the main conversation | file contents, command output, build logs and dead ends stay inside a worker's context |
| Four kinds of Subagent | a full-surface worker, a fork that inherits completed turns, a programmatic PTC worker and a read-only worker, chosen by task shape |
| Dispatch to another mode | hand a brief to any other installed agent preset and receive only its conclusion |
| Two-level approval gate | safe commands run untouched; dangerous ones raise a card in the main conversation |
| Corrections take effect immediately | a follow-up message stops the worker's current turn first instead of queueing behind the wrong work |
| Mode isolation | several modes can share one workspace; each narrows only its own sessions |
| Cross-session settings | pick a model per worker kind and set the parallelism limit, both in Settings |
| Automatic workspace permission repair | on Windows the one missing permission is added a

dsh-multitask README · How it differs from other modes：| | Main conversation (coordinator) | Subagent (worker) |
|---|---|---|
| Tool surface | read-only checks + delegation + result retrieval + interaction | full (write files, run commands, build, search…) |
| Context | your request + task briefs + conclusions | all the process data |
| Job | understand, translate, dispatch, verify, report | do the work |

What the coordinator keeps (a whitelist):
section: How it differs from other modes

text:
dsh-multitask README · How it differs from other modes：- **Read-only checks** — `read` `grep` `glob` `file_info`
- **Delegation** — `subagent` `subagent_fork` `subagent_ptc` `subagent_minimal`
- **Subagent control** — `send_message` `interrupt_agent` `list_agents`
- **Result retrieval** — `job_list` `job_output` `job_kill`
- **Orchestration** — `workflow`
- **Interaction and self-management** — `ask_user_question` `todo_write` `create_goal` `get_goal` `update_goal` `exit_plan_mode` `present` `skill`
section: How it differs from other modes

text: dsh-multitask README · How it differs from other modes：Anything not on that list is withheld by default — `write`, `edit`, `pwsh`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `read_image`, `ssh_*`, `task_board_*`, `plugin_manager`, and so on. The rule is a **complement**: withheld = currently visible − kept. Any tool the host adds later is therefore also withheld from the coordinator by default, with no change needed in this plugin.
section: How it differs from other modes

text: dsh-multitask README · How it differs from other modes：The read-only tools are kept on purpose: the coordinator is meant to **verify** a Subagent's claims independently instead of trusting them blindly.
section: How it differs from other modes

text:
dsh-multitask README · Mode isolation: it only narrows its own sessions：The narrowing is applied only to sessions whose live preset binding is this preset. A session belonging to another mode in the same workspace keeps its own tool roster and is not touched — so you can run several modes side by side without them eating each other's tools.

Switching a session out of the mode lifts the restriction again, and switching into it before the first turn narrows it before the first request is even made.
section: Mode isolation: it only narrows its own sessions

text: dsh-multitask README · Mode isolation: it only narrows its own sessions：`presetId` is that ownership key. If you change it to install variants side by side, each variant narrows only its own sessions; and if it no longer matches the registered preset id, **no** session is narrowed at all — the mode can look installed while quietly doing nothing.
section: Mode isolation: it only narrows its own sessions

text:
dsh-multitask README · Mode isolation: it only narrows its own sessions：When ownership cannot be read, the guard prefers **not** to narrow rather than risk narrowing a neighbour's session. The cost of a registry hiccup is therefore one possibly un-narrowed turn, never a broken neighbouring mode.

text:
dsh-multitask README · From the published package (recommended)：```
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-multitask
```

`--profile` is an **option** and cannot be dropped — `dsh plugin add dsh-multitask` fails outright with `error: required option '--profile <name>' not specified`. `<profile>` is the profile to install into: the desktop app owns one called `desktop`, and this checkout commonly uses `web`; if you are unsure, look at the directories under `~/.dsh/profiles/`.

dsh-multitask README · From the published package (recommended)：The package then lands in that profile's `node_modules`, and DSH **automatically** appends `dsh-multitask` to the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles` layer list (because this package declares `dsh.bundle.patch`). The bundled `cordis.patch.yml` inserts a bare package name with no absolute paths — so it works on any machine, any user name, any install location. **Restart the app afterwards** — bundle layers are composed at startup.
dsh-multitask README · From the published package (recommended)：You can also install it from the in-app **Plugins** page, which needs no command line.

dsh-multitask README · From the published package (recommended)：> **Desktop (Electron) note.** **Fully quit the app first** — pnpm rewrites the profile's `node_modules`, and the running app holding those files open will make it fail. The desktop app's own `dsh` launcher can manage `desktop`; a `dsh` **installed separately from npm** is refused outright (`error: profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron application`). In that case use the in-app **Plugins** page, or the source route below.

dsh-multitask README · From a source checkout：To run the sources in your working tree (edits without going through npm), **append** this block to the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, pointing at your local entry with an **absolute** `file://` URL:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: multitask
      name: 'file:///absolute/path/to/dsh-multitask/lib/index.js?v=6'
```

Two things to watch:

dsh-multitask README · From a source checkout：- **Spaces and `%` in the path must be percent-encoded** (common on Windows). Let a program encode it rather than typing it by hand — in PowerShell: `(New-Object System.Uri('H:\my repo\dsh-multitask\lib\index.js')).AbsoluteUri`.
- **The trailing `?v=N` is a cache key**, and it only means anything in this `file://` mode (see Development → "Making source edits take effect").

**Adding this row needs no restart**: DSH watches `cordis.patch.yml` and hot-reloads it.

---

dsh-multitask README · Usage：When creating a **new session**, pick **"Multitask 减震器模式"** in the mode selector, then just ask for what you want.

> The mode can be chosen **before a session's first turn starts**, and a session whose first turn has not yet started can still be switched into or out of it. What is frozen is a session that has **already started running its first turn** — that is an existing DSH constraint (the tool surface and prompt freeze on the first turn), not a limitation of this plugin.

dsh-multitask README · Usage：The coordinator translates your request into **self-contained** task briefs — a Subagent cannot see this conversation, so a brief must carry everything it needs (goal, verified current state, project conventions, safety rails, numbered tasks, conditional branches, stop conditions, report format). Independent briefs are dispatched **in parallel**, and the coordinator keeps working while they run.

---
dsh-multitask README · The four kinds of Subagent：The coordinator has four delegation paths, and the difference is mainly the **tool surface**:

dsh-multitask README · The four kinds of Subagent：| Delegation tool | Tool surface | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `subagent` | **full** | the default — writing code, running tests, editing files, execution work |
| `subagent_fork` | **full** + the **completed turns** of this conversation — it does **not** see the turn currently in flight, so a fact stated in the dispatching turn must be repeated in the brief | review and continuation — when the work must build on what is already established here |
| `subagent_ptc` | **PTC-collapsed**: only `run_code` is directly callable; every other tool is reached from inside a program via a generated SDK | programmatic bulk work — filtering, aggregating, or moving large data sets whose intermediate values should never enter the context |
| `subagent_minimal` | **read-only**: write and execute tools are removed, but it keeps `read` `grep` `glob` `read_image` `file_info` `skill` `todo_write` `present` and **can still search and fetch the web** | investigation, quick answers, fact-checking |

dsh-multitask README · The four kinds of Subagent：Pick by the shape of the task, not by habit. The four paths have different tool surfaces, and the choice is made per delegation in the coordinator persona (section `## Choosing which worker to delegate to`).

**Delegation is one level deep**: coordinator → worker, and a worker cannot delegate further. Jobs that need splitting are split by the coordinator into flat briefs.

dsh-multitask README · What a worker does not get：The four kinds also differ in **persona**, not only in tool surface. A fork worker is told that the seeded turns are the coordinator's work and not its own, so it reviews instead of pretending to have done it. A PTC worker is told that its closing message is the fallback channel if `run_code` breaks. The read-only worker is told it may search and fetch the web, so it does not report back that it "cannot look anything up".
section: What a worker does not get

text: dsh-multitask README · What a worker does not get：On top of that, five delegation tools — `subagent`, `subagent_fork`, `subagent_ptc`, `subagent_minimal`, `subagent_preset` — are removed from a worker's tool catalog outright, for every kind except the read-only worker. A worker therefore cannot delegate: the tool is **not there** rather than present-and-refused. This costs no capability, because the host's fixed depth of 1 would refuse every such call anyway; it only stops that schema being re-sent on every single request. The coordinator is untouched by this, and the read-only worker is narrowed by its own allowlist instead.
section: What a worker does not get

text: dsh-multitask README · What a worker does not get：This is **not a security boundary** — the real block is the host's depth limit. If it fails to install it degrades silently, leaving only a log line containing `WORKER-GUARD-SKIPPED`, and nothing is lost functionally. Its switch is the `worker-guard` row's `config.enabled` in `presets/multitask/composition.mjs` (which also accepts an additive `config.extraDeny`), and changing it requires a restart.
section: What a worker does not get

text: dsh-multitask README · What a worker does not get：If a worker's persona cannot be installed at all, that worker keeps the coordinator persona and the log shows `WORKER-PERSONA-SKIPPED`.
section: What a worker does not get

text: dsh-multitask README · Corrections stop the worker first：When the coordinator sends a follow-up to a running worker, the target's current turn is stopped **first**, and only then is the message delivered — it does not queue until the next step boundary. This matters because a single step can be one long tool call: a build, a dependency pull, a recursive scan. A correction that merely queued would let the wrong instruction run to completion before your new one was even read.

dsh-multitask README · Corrections stop the worker first：Stopping is not "the task was cancelled". The inbox and any descendants are kept, every fact already accepted is still in the session log, and only the one in-flight action is dropped. A correction to work that was on the right track therefore loses almost nothing — and the message may carry information the worker could not have had.

dsh-multitask README · Corrections stop the worker first：It only ever acts in the coordinator → worker direction. A message that a worker sends upward is not preceded by an interrupt, because that would cut the main conversation's own turn. If the interrupt fails, or the deployment exposes no interrupt capability, the message is still sent normally and corrections simply revert to queueing: you see an info line, not an error. Its only switch is the `interrupt-before-send` row's `config.enabled` in the composition, and changing it requires a restart.

dsh-multitask README · The read-only `file_info` tool：It is **this package's own tool** and the only self-authored tool on the coordinator's keep list. Its input is exactly one field: `paths`, an array of one or more path strings (up to 256), resolved by the filesystem backend with relative paths taken against the session working directory.

dsh-multitask README · The read-only `file_info` tool：The output is one entry per requested path — `requestedPath`, `resolvedPath`, `status`, `sizeKnown`, `sizeBytes` when known, and a `note` explaining an odd state — plus a `totals` block (`requested`, `files`, `directories`, `others`, `missing`, `errors`, `bytes`, `unknownSizes`, `complete`).

dsh-multitask README · The read-only `file_info` tool：`status` is one of `file`, `directory`, `other`, `missing` or `error`. A directory is reported **as a directory with no byte count**. A missing or uninspectable path is reported as such and is **never** reported as 0 bytes: when the backend cannot supply a size, `sizeKnown` is `false` and `sizeBytes` is absent rather than fabricated as zero.

dsh-multitask README · The read-only `file_info` tool：`totals.bytes` sums **only** the known sizes, `unknownSizes` counts the rest, and `complete` is true only when every requested path is a known-size regular file — so a partial sum never masquerades as a total.

dsh-multitask README · The read-only `file_info` tool：It never reads file contents and never modifies anything: it only resolves and stats each path. That is exactly why it is safe to keep in a mode whose entire point is keeping data out of the main conversation, and why the coordinator can use it to check a worker's claim ("five files, this many bytes") instead of trusting the report. It also serves the read-only worker, and it is deliberately **not** affected by the `DSH_MULTITASK_MULTI_MODE` switch.

dsh-multitask README · The read-only `file_info` tool：If the filesystem capability is unavailable at load time the tool is simply **not registered** — the model never sees a route that would fail — leaving a log line containing `FILE-INFO-SKIPPED`; success logs `FILE-INFO-ENGAGED`.

---

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：The four paths above are this mode's **own** workers. One more path reaches **outside** this mode:

| Delegation tool | Target | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `subagent_preset` | **any installed agent preset** (including third-party modes installed from the market) | when the job is genuinely something that other mode exists to do |

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：This is what makes the coordinator a layer between **you and every installed mode**: it picks one by reading what that mode says about itself, hands the brief over, and only receives the conclusion. The work happens in **that mode's worker**, not in your main conversation.

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：To use it, call with `list: true` first to read the roster (id, name, description, and whether each mode can currently compose a session), then choose by description. **The description is the only reliable statement of a mode's capabilities** — do not guess from the id. A mode marked `CANNOT RUN` is broken and must not be chosen.

Three boundaries:

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：- **The brief must be fully self-contained.** A cross-mode worker may not even share this mode's tool conventions, so it needs the background written out even more completely than an ordinary worker.
- **You cannot dispatch to this mode itself.** That would spawn a sub-coordinator, which the depth limit then refuses to let delegate — the call is rejected outright and points you at the four built-in paths.
- **Workers cannot dispatch further.** `subagent_preset` belongs to the coordinator; the tool refuses a worker's call itself, with its own message ("A delegated worker cannot dispatch further (delegation depth is fixed at 1)"), before any depth limit is consulted — deliberately, so the error names the real cause instead of surfacing a bare `depth 2 exceeds maxDepth 1` that looks unrelated. Splitting therefore always stays with the coordinator.

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：**A fourth boundary (measured, and worth knowing): a cross-mode worker is not governed by this mode's guards.**

In `setup()` a subagent is attached to the **target mode's** scope with `bindScopeParent(childKey, targetGenerationKey)`, and events like `agent/created` and `tools/pre-execute` reach only listeners **on that scope chain**. A cross-mode worker's chain is `[itself, target mode]` — it does **not** contain this mode. That cuts both ways:

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：- **The good side:** this mode's persona injection, read-only narrowing, and approval gate never leak into someone else's mode. A task you hand to a read-only mode will not be told "you have the full tool set" by this mode.
- **The side to keep in mind:** the **approval gate does not cover it either**. Upstream pins a child session's approval policy to `never`, so a cross-mode worker's dangerous operations are **refused outright** (fail-closed — never silently allowed), but **no card is raised to ask you**. It is governed by the target mode; if that mode has guards of its own, they apply.

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：So cross-mode dispatching is a **capability router, not a security proxy**. Work that needs this mode's two-level gate should still go to one of the four built-in paths.

dsh-multitask README · Dispatching to another mode：The provider is fixed to `spawn` and is not a configuration option: upstream requires a provider that can select another preset to declare the `agentPreset` capability **and** not inherit the parent's context. The built-in `spawn` satisfies both and `fork` does not. Hard-coding it avoids a class of capability error that would otherwise only surface at delegation time.

---

dsh-multitask README · Settings：Once installed, DSH's settings gain the following.

**The "Multitask" page — two cards**

dsh-multitask README · Settings：| Card | Field | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Model used by Subagents | `multitask.subagentModels[]` | the default model for each of the four worker kinds. Either "use one model for every Subagent" or per-kind; the default is "inherit coordinator". Applies only to sessions created **afterwards** |
| Subagent parallelism limit | `subagent.maxActiveSubagents` | **the same field** as the row in Settings → General, and it takes effect immediately |

dsh-multitask README · Settings：**The "General" page — two rows** (alongside the built-in language / appearance / developer-tools rows)

| Row | Field | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum recursion depth | `subagent.maxDepth` | host-level: applies to every mode, not just Multitask |
| Subagent parallelism limit | `subagent.maxActiveSubagents` | same; and it is the same value as the card on the Multitask page |

The session header also shows how many Subagents are currently running.

dsh-multitask README · Settings：The model card's **shape is derived, never stored**: all four kinds pointing at one route means "use one model for every Subagent", anything else means per-kind. Switching the shape creates no dirty state.

dsh-multitask README · How the settings page behaves：- The **Save / Discard bar** at the bottom of the Multitask page controls **only the model card**. The parallelism limit writes instantly, so editing it does not light up Save — that is not a broken button.
- Save and Discard stay **greyed out until the model mapping actually changes**.
- If the settings were changed elsewhere, a **banner** appears telling you to discard your draft and try again.
- The model dropdowns are populated from a **live catalogue**. While it loads you see a loading message; if it fails you see an error with a **Retry** button and the only choice is "Inherit coordinator"; and a saved model that is no longer advertised stays selectable with a "(saved but currently unavailable)" suffix, so you can still clear it.
- In "use one model for every Subagent" mode the first option is the placeholder **"Choose a model"**; picking it resets **all four** kinds to inherit. In per-kind mode each dropdown starts with **"Inherit coordinator (default)"**; selecting it removes that kind's entry.
- The two numeric rows (recursion depth, parallelism limit) accept **digits only** and are committed when the field loses focus o

dsh-multitask README · The session-header counter：- The session header shows how many Subagents are currently running, in three truthful states: a **count** when one or more are running, an explicit **"none running"** when the number is zero, and an explicit **"count unavailable"** rather than a guess when the projection cannot be read.
- It is **hidden entirely inside a sub-session** (a worker does not show a counter for its own siblings' children) and until the model catalogue has loaded.
- It sits **alongside** the host's own counter rather than replacing it, so seeing two numbers is expected.

dsh-multitask README · The Subagent parallelism limit：**There is only one value**: the host's `subagent.maxActiveSubagents`. It appears in **two places** in Settings (the card on the Multitask page, and a row in General), but both edit **the same field** — change it in either and the other follows immediately. This plugin adds no cap of its own, and there is no second layer cutting you off.

dsh-multitask README · The Subagent parallelism limit：That field's default is **8**: with no configuration, 8 is all you get. But 8 is a **default, not a ceiling** — **whatever you write is the limit**. To run N, set it to N — in either of the two Settings locations, or by giving the host row a config:

```yaml
- id: subagent
  config:
    maxActiveSubagents: 16
```

When the limit is exceeded, the extra delegations are dropped **before anything starts**, with this error, verbatim:

dsh-multitask README · The Subagent parallelism limit：```
Error: subagent limit reached (active child limit: 8); wait for an existing child to finish or complete this work with the current agents
```

dsh-multitask README · The Subagent parallelism limit：**The refusal is the host's.** It is neither a broken plugin nor a fault: the host raises it while handing out slots, before any Subagent is created — so you get a plain error rather than a Subagent id. The fix is to **wait for existing Subagents to finish**, or **merge several tasks into one brief** for a single Subagent. Do not retry the same fan-out unchanged.

dsh-multitask README · The Subagent parallelism limit：The count is "**total live Subagents under one main Agent**", not just the ones you started in the same round: a worker that has finished its brief but has not exited **still occupies a slot**. So the safe pattern is "dispatch a batch → let them all finish → dispatch the next batch".

dsh-multitask README · The Subagent parallelism limit：> ⚠️ **"I dispatched 10 and they all succeeded" does not prove the limit was raised.** That is blocking / serial execution: one runs at a time, and the next starts only after the previous ends, so **the live count never exceeded 1**. Only a fan-out **inside a single message** actually competes for slots. To tell parallel from serial, look at how many Subagents are running at one instant, not at how many you dispatched in total.

---

dsh-multitask README · Approving dangerous operations：In this mode all the real work is done by Subagents, and DSH turns their approval chain off by default (the policy is pinned to `never`, and the model is additionally told to self-censor). This plugin wires it back up as a **two-level gate**:

dsh-multitask README · Approving dangerous operations：| Level | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Level 1 (deterministic rules) | safe commands **run directly, without interrupting you** — no extra model request, no change to the sandbox |
| Level 2 (relay to the parent session) | dangerous commands **raise an approval card in the main conversation** for you to allow or reject — reusing the existing approval panel, with no new UI |

dsh-multitask README · Approving dangerous operations：Level 1 covers what the sandbox cannot express: destructive commands **inside** the workspace (`rm -rf .`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`), non-file dangers (`git push --force`, `npm publish`, `curl | bash`, privilege escalation, execution-policy changes), and writes outside the workspace. A missed pattern behaves exactly like having no plugin at all, so Level 1 can only **add** a prompt — never remove protection.

dsh-multitask README · Approving dangerous operations：**The red line**: all of this is enabled **only in interactive sessions** — the parent session's approval policy must be `ask`. Headless and unattended deployments rely on `never` to guarantee they are never left waiting for an answer that will not come, and this plugin does nothing at all in that environment.

dsh-multitask README · How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review：DSH has an experimental feature, Auto Review: it switches the permission preset to `auto`, so **every native tool call** (and every inner call inside a PTC program) is first risk-classified by a reviewer running the same model. It and this plugin are **two independent gates** on the same chain, enforced by two separate pieces of code.

While it is on, **this plugin's Level 1 yields** — the reviewer is the authority for that session:
section: How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review

text:
dsh-multitask README · How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review：| Reviewer decision | Result |
|---|---|
| allow (low risk, or a medium action with explicit authorisation) | runs immediately — **this plugin does not raise `ask`**, so you are not asked twice |
| deny, with the approval policy at `ask` | the reviewer returns `ask` itself, which reaches this plugin's Level-2 relay → a card appears in the main conversation for you |
| deny, with the policy at `never` | the reviewer's denial is final; `AUTO_REVIEW_DENIED` goes straight back to the Subagent |
| reviewer failure | treated as `deny` (fail-closed) — never a silent allow |
section: How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review

text:
dsh-multitask README · How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review：**With Auto Review off, behaviour is completely unchanged**: this plugin raises `ask` from the rule table as before. The test is "is this session's permission preset `auto`", the same test the reviewer uses, so the two sides can never disagree about who is in charge. The switch is `yieldToAutoReview` (default `true`); pass `false` to keep prompting even when the reviewer is in charge.

⚠️ Two boundaries worth knowing:
section: How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review

text:
dsh-multitask README · How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review：- **The reviewer does not review the outer `run_code`**, only the inner calls inside it; a `subagent_ptc` worker can produce Node side effects directly from its program. For a PTC worker, **the sandbox is still the last line**, not the reviewer.
- **Review costs extra tokens**: every reviewed call is a full model request.

Authorisation is **one-shot every time**: "Allow once" authorises that call only, and the same call prompts again next time. There is no "always allow".
section: How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review

text: dsh-multitask README · How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review：**With a background dispatch whose turn has ended**, the first relay fails (it needs the parent session to have an open turn). The plugin then sends a message from that Subagent into the main conversation, naming which child session it is, what it wants to run, and where to answer — and **that message itself wakes the idle parent session**, so the plugin immediately retries the relay against the turn it just opened. In practice an ordinary approval card therefore appears in the main conversation within seconds; answer it there.
section: How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review

text: dsh-multitask README · How this interacts with Experimental Auto Review：Only if that retry also fails (the window elapses, 10 seconds by default) do you need to open the child session named in the message and decide there. **The message is not an approval** — the message channel carries no approval result, so reading it as a go-ahead would bypass the gate; until you answer, that call stays blocked.

text: dsh-multitask README · Which commands it stops for：Level 1 is a **pattern table, not an AI review**. It only ever *adds* a prompt: a command no pattern matches is equivalent to not having this module at all. The families it matches:

dsh-multitask README · Which commands it stops for：- **Recursive / forced deletion** — `rm -rf`, `Remove-Item -Recurse` / `-Force`, `del /q`, `rd /s`
- **Disk and boot operations** — `format X:`, `diskpart` / `fdisk` / `parted` / `mkfs`, `dd of=`, `bcdedit` / `bootrec`
- **Power state** — `shutdown`, `Restart-Computer`, `Stop-Computer`, `reboot`
- **Git history and remote destruction** — `push --force` / `--force-with-lease` / `-f`, `reset --hard`, `clean -f`, `filter-branch` / `filter-repo`, `remote remove`, `checkout -- .`
- **Package publishing** — `npm` / `pnpm` / `yarn` / `bun` `publish` / `unpublish`, `cargo publish` / `yank`, `twine upload`, `dotnet nuget push`, `docker push`
- **Privilege escalation** — `sudo` / `doas` / `pkexec` / `runas` / `gsudo`, `Start-Process -Verb RunAs`, `Set-ExecutionPolicy`
- **System mutation** — accounts and groups, the registry, services, scheduled tasks, WMI, the firewall, ownership changes
- **Remote-code execution** — `Invoke-Expression` / `iex`, piping into a shell, `-EncodedCommand`, `certutil -urlcache`, `bitsadmin`, forced process kill

dsh-multitask README · Which commands it stops for：Deliberately **not** matched, so do not "fix" it into prompting on harmless commands: dry runs such as `git clean -nd`; `icacls` on a path without a mutation flag; bare `net user` and `wmic process list`; `chmod +x`; reading credential files; `ls /etc`. Writing **outside the workspace** is a separate check, made on the write tools' `file_path` rather than on command text.

dsh-multitask README · Which commands it stops for：Quoted text is judged by its context: inside `-Pattern` / `-match` / `-like` / `-eq` / `Select-String` the command text is not treated as code, so searching *for* a dangerous string does not prompt — while the body of `-Command` / `-c` deliberately **is** treated as code, so a dangerous command inside it does prompt.

dsh-multitask README · What the approval card shows：The card may be shown a path that contains `..`. When that changes where the path really lands, the reason line and both displayed descriptions carry the **resolved target** next to the literal one, together with the id of the rule that matched — so you approve the destination, not just the spelling.

Authorisation is **one-shot**: "Allow once" authorises that call only, and the same call prompts again next time. There is no "always allow".

dsh-multitask README · What the approval card shows：Level 1 never pre-empts an upstream decision. It runs **after** the downstream handlers and only upgrades an `allow` into an `ask`; if something earlier in the chain already said `ask` or `deny`, that verdict stands and this module's card does not appear — so a write may be stopped by a different prompt than this module's.

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：**The mode does not appear in the new-session selector.** First confirm the plugin row is actually installed (visible in the plugins list, and not `disabled`), then restart the app. If it is still missing, look in the log for warnings beginning with `dsh-multitask` — they name the cause (registry absent, composition invalid, id held by an earlier module instance, and so on).

**A Subagent fails to run any command at all**, with this error, verbatim:

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：```
Error: SetNamedSecurityInfoW failed (Win32 5): grantWrite(<workspace path>)
```

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：This is not about concurrency (it reproduces with a single Subagent running) and not about the command (even `Get-Location` fails). It is a **directory-permission precondition on the workspace folder**: DSH's ACL sandbox must write a security descriptor onto the session's writable root, and that call includes a mandatory integrity label. The label lives in the SACL, so the call additionally needs **WRITE_OWNER**, while the owner's implicit rights cover only `READ_CONTROL` and `WRITE_DAC`. A folder that grants you only *Modify* therefore lacks it and the call fails — which is why a workspace under your user profile works with no setup, while a folder created directly under a drive root (inheriting only Modify) does not.

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：**The repair is already automatic.** At session start this plugin checks the workspace folder and, if `WRITE_OWNER` is missing, **adds exactly that one permission** (a non-inherited `TakeOwnership`) and stops. It needs no approval and no elevation, and you should **never** widen a folder to *Full control* for this — that would additionally hand over the right to change permissions and take ownership, far beyond what is needed.

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：If a Subagent is still refused, the automatic grant did not land: the folder is **owned by another account**, or it is **not writable** by this process. In that case, treat it as your decision — it is the specific, fixable cause, with the folder named. **Read-only tools are unaffected**, so content and file-metadata tasks are always delegable.

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：**You hit the parallelism limit.** See "The Subagent parallelism limit" above; the refusal is the host's. Wait for existing Subagents, or merge tasks into one brief.

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：**A worker stopped mid-sentence and the turn looks like it crashed.** A single reply has a hard ceiling on how much it can emit. Hitting it ends the turn with reason `max-tokens`, and from the outside that looks exactly like a crash. **It is not context exhaustion.** The fix is not to shrink what the worker should read; it is to split what it should write. Workers are told to keep one write under roughly 400–500 lines and to resume from the tail of a truncated file rather than starting over, which is why a large deliverable often arrives as a skeleton followed by successive edits. If a worker reports the same construct failing twice, that is a deliberate stop signal, not stubbornness: it will report the location and the verbatim error instead of varying the fix. The recovery is to start a **fresh** worker on that one spot rather than sending the same worker another retry instruction.

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：**No approval card appeared.** First check that the session's approval policy is `ask` (a headless configuration is `never`, and then this plugin stays entirely out of the way). If you dispatched in the background and the turn has ended, see the paragraph beginning "With a background dispatch whose turn has ended" in "Approving dangerous operations".

dsh-multitask README · Common problems：**Source edits have no effect.** You must **restart the app**. Bumping `?v=N` in the profile patch alone is a no-op for a row that is already running: the loader only sees that its name changed, so it neither reloads the module nor restarts it. See "Making source edits take effect" in [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md).

dsh-multitask README · When the automatic permission repair runs：- **It is Windows-only.** On macOS and Linux the module is completely inert and registers nothing.
- **It runs for any session whose resolved sandbox mode is `workspace-write`, delegated Subagents included.** A `read-only` or `danger-full-access` session gets no grant, and the skip is logged.
  > Earlier it only handled root sessions, on the grounds that Subagents share the parent's cwd. But when the parent is not yet in Multitask at creation time (it is switched in before the first turn, or the worker comes from cross-mode dispatch), the parent's one chance is already gone and every worker was skipped — so nobody granted anything. The criterion is now "has this cwd been handled": a parent that already granted costs one set lookup, and a parent that missed is covered by the first worker that appears. Switching the preset in before the first turn also triggers a check.
- **The folder it touches is the session's own working directory**, not "the writable root" in the abstract. No cwd means no action.
- **What it adds:** exactly one `Allow` entry for the **current user's** SID with the single right `TakeOwnership` and no
section: When the automatic permission repair runs

text: dsh-multitask README · Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass：The host's three entries **inherit only at creation time** and are never propagated back into subdirectories that already exist. A workspace carried over from an older version therefore stays **half-done** for a long time: the root has all three, while the existing `.git` / `docs` / `lib` / `presets` / `test` have none of them; only directories created after the root was fixed are complete. That is exactly what was measured — the root complete, those seven older directories with none, a newly created `research` complete.
section: Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass

text: dsh-multitask README · Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass：**The symptom differs from the one above — do not confuse them.** Once the root has `WRITE_OWNER` the session itself starts, but the sandbox shell runs at **Low integrity with a restricted token** (the restricting list holds only the logon SID / `Everyone` / the capability SID / the temp-directory SID, and **not `Authenticated Users`**), so creating a file inside an unstamped existing directory is refused. The canonical one-liner is:
section: Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass

text:
dsh-multitask README · Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass：```
fatal: Unable to create '.../.git/index.lock': Permission denied
```

usually followed by `[sandbox: file access denied under workspace-write mode]`. **The approval card has nothing to do with it** — approval only decides whether to ask, it does not permit stepping outside the sandbox, and approving once does not make that write land.
section: Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass

text: dsh-multitask README · Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass：**The repair is automatic again, and it runs serially right after the previous step:** once the root's `WRITE_OWNER` is in place, the same module runs three `icacls` actions over the existing objects (the path still comes only from an environment variable, never spliced into the script): first grant the current user `(WO)` on the whole tree (writing the integrity label needs `WRITE_OWNER` on the object), then `/inheritance:e` so existing objects re-inherit the parent's inheritable entries (that is where the capability ACE comes from — **the capability SID is never hardcoded**), and finally `/setintegritylevel` to write the same Low label the host uses. The order cannot be reversed: without `(WO)`, neither of the last two can be written.
section: Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass

text:
dsh-multitask README · Existing subdirectories are not stamped retroactively: that needs a second pass：- **A read-only screen comes first:** it reads `icacls` for each **direct** subdirectory, and if all of them already carry a `Mandatory Label` it prints `SUB-OK` and returns, **without a single write**. After the first repair a session only pays for those few read-only calls.
- **It can be switched off on its own** with `config.autoRepairStampedChildren: false`, **independent of** `autoGrantWriteOwner` (one covers the root, the other the existing objects).
- **The cost, stated plainly:** the first run on an old workspace walks the whole tree and adds one `(WO,S)` ACE to every existing object; a big tree (`node_modules`) is noticeably slower the first time and short-circuits afterwards thanks to the screen above. The default limit is `120` seconds.
- **A failure is fail-open:** it is logged, never thrown, and never allowed to block the session — the worst case is the behaviour you have today (subdirectories still refused).
- **Outcome markers** you can grep: `MULTITASK-WORKSPACE-ACL-SUB-OK`, `-SUB-REPAIRED`, `-SUB-SKIPPED`, `-SUB-FAILED`.
- **It does not invent policy:** the capabi

text:
dsh-multitask README · Verifying that it actually works：| You say | Expected |
|---|---|
| "Read package.json yourself and tell me the version." | ✅ succeeds (read-only checks are kept) |
| "Run `git status` yourself." | ❌ the call is impossible — the tool is not in its visible set |
| "Delegate to a Subagent to run `git status` and report the conclusion." | ✅ the Subagent runs it and brings back only the conclusion |
| "Delegate to a Subagent to read package.json and report the file name and size." | ✅ the read-only route always works (`read` / `file_info`) |

dsh-multitask README · Verifying that it actually works：With a log sink attached, the log shows which tools were actually withheld — grep for `dsh-multitask` **without** the trailing colon, because the informational "engaged / withheld N tools" lines use the plain `dsh-multitask:` prefix while the guard warnings carry their module name, e.g. `dsh-multitask/coordinator-guard:`, `dsh-multitask/minimal-guard:`, `dsh-multitask/subagent-mode:` or `dsh-multitask/worker-persona:`. Grepping for `dsh-multitask:` alone will **miss exactly the warnings that tell you a guard failed to engage**. ⚠️ This deployment does **not** persist that channel (measured: the only occurrences left in session logs are source text echoed in conversation), so failing to grep it does **not** mean nothing was withheld — the judge is that calling those tools fails:

dsh-multitask README · Verifying that it actually works：```
dsh-multitask: coordinator scope engaged — withheld N tool(s): edit, pwsh, read_image, ssh_exec, ...
```

The approval gate's preconditions and its verification steps — including the fallback path for background dispatches — are in [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md), under "Verifying that it actually works" and "Approving dangerous operations".

dsh-multitask README · Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other：This mode has a quiet but important property: **a claim from either side must be grounded in evidence — neither gets by on "I remember" or "I assumed".** It does not depend on a model being asked to review itself; it rests on two mechanisms:
section: Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other

text:
dsh-multitask README · Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other：- **When the coordinator's premise is wrong, the worker pushes back.** The worker persona requires it to ground every claim in what it actually observed, never to report a result it did not obtain, and — on hitting a blocking situation — to stop and report it verbatim instead of improvising a workaround. So when a premise in the brief does not hold, it names the premise that does not.
- **Whatever a worker reports, the coordinator re-checks independently.** Keeping the read-only tools (`read` / `grep` / `glob` / `file_info`) is exactly what lets it go and look for itself rather than treating the report as fact.
section: Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other

text:
dsh-multitask README · Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other：In other words: the worker is not there to agree with the brief, and the coordinator may not promote a report into a conclusion — **neither side accepts the other's assertion on trust.**

That is not inferred from the design intent; it was measured. The three screenshots below are consecutive views of one end-to-end test report, and the three mistakes in it were **all corrected by a worker**:
section: Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other

text:
dsh-multitask README · Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other：- **Misjudged the asar as unreadable.** The coordinator first concluded "a packed archive means the sources are unreadable" and told the worker to back off; the worker contradicted it — `ripgrep` reads `.asar` as text, and inside is the real, commented source. The coordinator re-checked, confirmed the worker was right and it was wrong, and got source-level answers to six of seven questions.
- **Wrote the wrong escalation value.** The coordinator wrote "the narrowest escalation that is still wider", which the native worker read as `workspace-write` — the mode it was already in. Line-by-line verification of the source left no room for interpretation: `app.asar:911220` reads `if (mode === effectiveMode) return effectiveMode;` — **the same level is a silent no-op that never requests approval**; `:911221` reads `is not strictly wider than` (a level that is not wider throws outright); and the ladder has exactly one rung (`:911150-151`, `"workspace-write": ["danger-full-access"]`). The second refusal (byte-for-byte identical to the first) was therefore purely a defect in the brief, and it burned an ap

text: dsh-multitask README · Self-correction: each side's conclusions get checked by the other：One more case from the same run: a file appeared that no brief had asked for, and two independent lines of evidence agreed it was written by a PTC worker probing its own native tool permissions — it deliberately picked a path that looked nonexistent, expected a refusal, and the write succeeded; seeing the file in a concurrent call, it first misattributed it to a sibling worker, and later **withdrew its own "it was not me"**. An independent forensic worker measured the file's NTFS creation time and found it matching that account to the millisecond, inside a 15.6-second window between two other writes — while stating plainly that the filesystem cannot attribute authorship. The evidence established that the file belonged to this session; attribution came from the worker's own account, and that distinction was not glossed over.

dsh-multitask README · Tunables (profile)：Override by **id**, appending after the `dsh-multitask` `insert` block (a later entry with the same id wins):

```yaml
- id: multitask
  config:
    presetId: multitask          # change this to install several variants side by side
    order: 5                     # position in the mode selector

`enabled: false` turns the whole plugin off (no preset is declared, and the mode disappears from the selector).
dsh-multitask README · Tunables (profile)：The remaining switches live in the `config` of the corresponding rows in `presets/multitask/composition.mjs`:

dsh-multitask README · Tunables (profile)：| Row | Effect of disabling |
|---|---|
| `subagent-mode` | the PTC presentation is off, and `subagent_ptc` degrades to the same native surface as `subagent` |
| `minimal-guard` | the read-only worker is **not narrowed at all** — it sees every tool the composition registers, including write-capable ones and anything other plugins add. There is no static layer behind it any more (DSH 0.2.1-rc.2 removed the delegation row's `toolFilter`), so this switch is a **security downgrade**, not a convenience. Because the worker guard deliberately skips the read-only worker, switching `minimal-guard` off also makes the five delegation tools visible to it again |
| `worker-guard` | the five delegation tools are no longer removed from worker catalogs; only tokens are wasted, since the host's depth limit still refuses every call. It also accepts an additive `config.extraDeny` |
| `interrupt-before-send` | corrections go back to queueing at the next step boundary instead of stopping the target's current turn |
| `approval-gate` | dangerous operations no longer prompt (back to default DSH behaviour) |
| `workspace-acl` | `WRITE_OWNER` is no longer granted a

dsh-multitask README · Tunables (profile)：The environment variable `DSH_MULTITASK_MULTI_MODE=0` removes the `subagent_ptc` and `subagent_minimal` delegation paths (and their two keep-list entries) in one step, without touching the original `subagent` / `subagent_fork`. It does **not** unmount the PTC presentation row: `subagent-mode` — the row that performs the collapse — is mounted unconditionally. Because no `multitask_ptc` worker then exists, the collapse has nothing to act on, so the practical effect is as if the presentation were off, but the row itself is still there. To turn the presentation off for real, disable the `subagent-mode` row. Only `0`, `false` and `off` disable the variable's switch — any other value, including a typo, leaves it enabled. It is read at module load, so it needs an app restart.

dsh-multitask README · The approval-gate row's switches：The profile patch cannot reach this row's `config` — the host half applies only the top-level switches, and only to the `coordinator-guard` row. To change it, edit its `config` in `presets/multitask/composition.mjs` and restart the app:

dsh-multitask README · The approval-gate row's switches：| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `classify` | `true` | Master switch for Level 1 (the deterministic rule table). `false` = dangerous commands are no longer stopped to ask; the Level-2 relay still runs |
| `relay` | `true` | Master switch for Level 2 (the relay). `false` = a Subagent's request no longer reaches the main conversation |
| `relayRetryWindowMs` | `10000` | How long to wait for the parent session to open a turn when the turn was just closed (ms). `0` disables the retry (back to notice-only) |
| `notifyOnRelayFailure` | `true` | The fallback notice when the relay fails. `false` turns it off: the relay still proceeds when the parent turn is **already open**, but when the turn is **closed** the notice is the only thing that can wake the parent session, so the retry cannot run and the request stays blocked until you answer in the child session |
| `extraDangerPatterns` | `[]` | Extra danger patterns, each `{ id, re }` or a bare string / regex. It can only **add** a prompt, never remove one |
| `safePatterns` | `[]` | Extra "match but do not ask" allow-patterns. ⚠️ This is a **prompt-suppressing** chann

dsh-multitask README · The approval-gate row's switches：`extraDangerPatterns` / `shellTools` / `fileTools` are **additive**: missing one only means those cases are not examined (equivalent to not having this module), and it never lets through something this module would have asked about. `safePatterns` is **subtractive**: it cancels a danger this module has **already** judged, which is why it is deliberately empty by default — a mistake there is a silent permit, not one fewer prompt.

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：The temp directory is the **scratch paper every process shares** — DSH itself creates `dsh-subagent-*` and `dsh-acl-locks` there. A worker writing intermediate artifacts there is ordinary work; prompting for it only trains you to click "Allow" without looking, which weakens the prompts that matter. Two cases are exempt by default:

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：- **writing into** the temp directory (a `write` / `edit` whose `file_path` lands under an allowed root);
- **deleting only inside** it (under the strict conditions below).

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：The default roots are derived from `TEMP` / `TMP` / `TMPDIR` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp` (no `node:os` import — this package's preset modules are dependency-free), and `/tmp` is added on every platform. Setting this field **replaces** that whole list: if you list only your own cache directory, the platform temp directory is no longer exempt. To extend rather than replace, list the temp roots again together with your own. An empty array turns the exemption off entirely, so even the temp directory prompts.

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：**The deletion exemption is deliberately strict** — four conditions, all required: no shell metacharacters (`,`, newline, and `;` `|` `&` `` ` `` `$` `>` `<`); at least one absolute path argument; **every** path argument under an allowed root; and no relative path arguments, with no `..` segment anywhere in a path. So:

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `rm -rf /tmp/x` | no prompt |
| `rm -rf /tmp/x /home/u` | **prompts** — one path is outside the roots |
| `rm -rf C:\Windows` | **prompts** |
| `rm -rf $env:TEMP\x` | **prompts** — it contains `$`, so no exemption |
| `Remove-Item -Recurse C:\Windows` | **prompts** |
| `Remove-Item -LiteralPath "/tmp/a","C:\Windows" -Recurse -Force` | **prompts** — comma-glued, the two paths have no space between them |
| `rm -rf /tmp/../../../etc` | **prompts** — `..` walks the path outside the root |
| `rm -rf /tmp/a ..` | **prompts** — a relative path argument deletes the parent of the working directory |

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：The last three rows are three real holes measured on 1.2.10 (comma gluing, `..` traversal, and relative path arguments all rode the exemption); the fix and its regressions land from 1.2.12.

The reason is blunt: one wrong exemption lets an entire dangerous command through, while one extra prompt costs a click. **This tier only decides whether to interrupt you, never what the sandbox allows** — where a worker can actually write is still decided by DSH's sandbox and ACL.

dsh-multitask README · Temp-directory exemption (`autoApproveTempRoots`)：Source edits take effect only after a **restart**.

dsh-multitask README · Uninstalling：If you installed from the package manager, let it do the work: `dsh plugin --profile <profile> remove dsh-multitask`, or uninstall from the **Plugins** page.
If you installed from a source checkout, delete the whole `- insert: - id: multitask` block from the profile patch.

dsh-multitask README · Uninstalling：Either way the mode disappears from the selector for **new** sessions (running sessions are unaffected), and **no restart is needed** — DSH hot-reloads that patch, and the plugin unregisters its own preset declaration on unload. To **suspend** it temporarily instead, add `disabled: true` to that row.

dsh-multitask/
├── package.json                        # dsh.bundle.patch → inserts the host row on install; dsh.client → the browser half

The cost is that a few constants are duplicated, and changing one means changing the other.

dsh-multitask README · Making source edits take effect：**Restart the app after editing the sources.** This package lives outside the HMR-watched root, so Node's ESM cache keeps serving the old module; and although the profile patch itself *is* hot-reloaded, **bumping `?v=N` on a row that is already running only changes its name** — the loader takes the name-only branch and does not reload. A fresh process reading that row for the first time is what actually picks up your latest source.

dsh-multitask README · Making source edits take effect：Two related traps: a relative import does **not** inherit the entry's query (this package propagates it explicitly, so one bump refreshes the whole module graph), and "delete and re-add within one save" does not work either (the comparison is by id, so it is still the same row) — you must delete, let it settle, then add it back.

dsh-multitask README · Known boundaries：- **The mode is only selectable in a new session.** A running session cannot switch in.
- **What the coordinator cannot see, it cannot verify.** Keeping read-only tools is exactly what lets it check a Subagent's claims; remove `read` / `grep` / `glob` and that ability is gone.
- **Self-correction is a dependable tendency, not a hard guarantee.** That all three mistakes were pushed back on is a measured result, and it rests on two mechanisms being present **at the same time**: the worker persona forbidding results it did not obtain, and the coordinator keeping its read-only tools. With either one gone, the correction may simply not happen.
- **Delegation depth is 1.** A worker cannot delegate further; very large jobs must be split by the coordinator into parallel briefs.
- **PTC's "collapse" is a presentation collapse, not a capability cut — by design, not a defect.** The direct surface of `subagent_ptc` really is just `run_code`, but the SDK binding table remains fully callable from inside a program; remove it and PTC is an empty shell.
